lessons.title: Study Session 1: Choosing Indicators That Measure What Actually Matters

blocks.text: Introduction Bolanle Adeyemi had spent two years reporting a steady rise in the number of pregnant women attending at least one antenatal visit at the clinics her maternal health programme supported in Ilorin, a number that climbed reliably every quarter while the rate of dangerous delivery complications, the outcome the programme actually existed to reduce, showed no matching improvement at all. 1.0 Learning Outcomes By the end of this study session, you should be able to: Explain what research found about selecting indicators that genuinely reflect a management objective. Distinguish an indicator that is easy to count from one that actually reflects the intended outcome. Apply a set of criteria for testing whether a proposed indicator measures what a programme is actually trying to achieve. Recognise when a rising indicator is being mistaken for genuine programme progress. 2.0 Main Content 2.1 A Number That Kept Climbing, A Problem That Did Not Move Bolanle Adeyemi coordinates monitoring for a maternal health programme operating across a cluster of clinics in Ilorin, and for two years running, the quarterly figure she reported with the most confidence was the count of women attending at least one antenatal visit. That figure rose every single quarter. The rate of severe delivery complications recorded at the same clinics, the specific outcome the programme had been funded to reduce, stayed essentially flat across the same period. 2.2 What Makes an Indicator Actually Useful In 2011, the researchers Ayesha Tulloch, Hugh Possingham and Kerrie Wilson published a study in Biological Conservation examining how conservation managers select indicators for tracking whether their management actions are actually succeeding. Their finding, developed for conservation programmes but directly transferable to programme monitoring generally, was that a genuinely useful indicator must be closely and specifically linked to the actual management objective, sensitive enough to detect real change when it occurs, and interpretable without ambiguity, rather than chosen primarily because it happens to be convenient or inexpensive to count. 2.3 Testing a Proposed Indicator Before Adopting It Checking Whether an Indicator Is Actually Linked to the Objective Asking directly whether a proposed indicator would genuinely move if the programme's actual objective were achieved, rather than assuming a connection because the indicator sits somewhere in the same general subject area, is the specific test the Tulloch, Possingham and Wilson research recommends applying before adopting any indicator. Checking Whether an Indicator Can Actually Detect Change Confirming that an indicator is sensitive enough to move when a real improvement or decline actually happens, rather than remaining essentially flat regardless of underlying progress, separates an indicator worth tracking from one that will simply sit unchanged no matter what the programme does. 2.4 Key Practices Ask whether a proposed indicator would genuinely move if the actual objective were achieved. Confirm an indicator is sensitive enough to detect real change when it occurs. Pair a simple activity count with at least one indicator closer to the actual outcome. Question an indicator chosen mainly because it is convenient or inexpensive to collect. 2.5 A Worked Example: Bolanle's Revised Indicator Set Bolanle kept the antenatal visit count, since it remained genuinely useful for tracking clinic reach, but added a second indicator alongside it, the proportion of deliveries attended by a skilled birth attendant, a measure sitting far closer to the programme's actual objective of reducing dangerous complications. Within two quarters, the new indicator revealed something the visit count alone had never shown: skilled attendance at delivery had actually stagnated in two of the four clinics, despite steady antenatal attendance at both. The visit count had never been wrong as a measurement. It had simply never been able to see the specific problem the programme most needed to catch. 2.6 Common Pitfalls Adopting an indicator because it is easy to count, without first checking whether it would actually move if the underlying objective were achieved, produces a monitoring system that looks active while remaining blind to the exact problem the programme exists to solve. A number climbing steadily does not by itself confirm that anything underneath it has actually improved. 2.7 The Objective Had Always Been the Same. The Measure of It Had Not. Bolanle's programme had never actually shifted its purpose from reducing delivery complications to counting antenatal visits. The visit count had simply been standing in for a goal it was never specific enough to represent. 3.0 Study Session Summary and Conclusion In this study session, you learned to test whether a proposed indicator is genuinely linked to a programme's actual objective before adopting it. Study Session 2 turns from choosing the right indicator to building a data collection routine trustworthy enough to report it from.

Reflect and Grow — Self-Assessment 1. Think of an indicator your own programme or team currently tracks. Would it genuinely move if the actual underlying objective were achieved, or is it measuring something adjacent instead? 2. Identify one indicator you currently rely on mainly because it is easy to collect, and name a second indicator closer to the actual outcome that could be tracked alongside it. Practical Output: Practical Output A short written test of one real programme indicator against the linkage, sensitivity and interpretability criteria from this session, with a proposed second indicator if the first is found lacking. 7.0 References and Further Reading Tulloch, A.I.T., Possingham, H.P., & Wilson, K.A. (2011). Wise selection of an indicator for monitoring the success of management actions. Biological Conservation, 144(1), 141 to 154. Optional further reading, curriculum-team reviewed: 1 Chronicles 28:9, on the Lord searching all hearts and understanding every plan and thought. Qur'an, Surah Al-Anbiya 21:47, on the scales of justice being set up so that no soul is wronged in the least, even the weight of a mustard seed.
Evidence to keep Keep a written note, worksheet, reflection or practical output from this study session. Your progress should show real learning before the quiz.

lessons.title: Study Session 2: Building a Data Collection Routine That Can Be Trusted

blocks.text: Introduction Furaha Massawe compiled the quarterly farmer training attendance figures for an agricultural extension programme in Moshi from five field officers' registers, and discovered only when the totals refused to add up correctly that two of the five had been recording rounded estimates rather than actual daily headcounts for months. 1.0 Learning Outcomes By the end of this study session, you should be able to: Explain what research found about the effect of a formal data quality assessment on a data collection system. Apply a simple routine check for identifying where a data collection process is actually breaking down. Recognise the specific signs that a data collection routine cannot yet be trusted. 2.0 Main Content 2.1 Five Registers, Two of Them Guessing Furaha Massawe coordinates monitoring for an agricultural extension programme working with smallholder farmers around Moshi, drawing quarterly attendance figures from five field officers' handwritten registers. Reconciling one quarter's totals against a spot count from a single training session, she found two of the five officers had been recording attendance in rounded estimates, twenty, thirty, forty, rather than an actual daily headcount, for at least three consecutive quarters. 2.2 What a Formal Data Quality Check Actually Surfaces In 2019, the researchers Jennifer Yourkavitch, Debra Prosnitz and Samantha Herrera published a study in the Journal of Global Health examining data quality assessments conducted across community health programmes in five African countries. Their finding was that a first formal data quality assessment reliably surfaced specific, previously unnoticed weaknesses in each site's data collection process, and that identifying those weaknesses directly prompted concrete fixes, including revised collection tools, additional supervisor training, and stronger routine supervision of frontline data recorders. 2.3 Checking a Collection Routine Before Trusting It Spot-Checking a Sample of Records Against Reality Comparing a small sample of recorded figures directly against an independent count of the same event, rather than assuming a register is accurate simply because it has been consistently submitted, is the specific practice the Yourkavitch, Prosnitz and Herrera research found surfaced real weaknesses that had gone unnoticed for months. Watching for Numbers That Are Suspiciously Round Noticing when recorded figures cluster suspiciously around round numbers rather than showing the ordinary variation a genuine headcount produces is a simple, low-cost signal that a record may be an estimate rather than an actual count. 2.4 Key Practices Spot-check a small sample of records against an independent count of the same event. Watch for recorded figures that cluster suspiciously around round numbers. Standardise the exact recording tool and method used across every field officer. Schedule a formal data quality check on a fixed routine rather than only after a problem appears. 2.5 A Worked Example: Furaha's Quarterly Spot Check Furaha introduced a standard headcount slip to be completed at every training session and began attending one randomly selected session per officer per quarter to compare her own count against the submitted figure, replacing the informal trust she had previously placed in whichever register arrived on time. The two officers who had been estimating adjusted within a single quarter once the standard slip and the spot-check routine were both in place, and the following quarter's totals reconciled cleanly against Furaha's own independent counts for the first time in over a year. The problem had never been the officers' honesty. It had been a collection routine with no built-in way of checking itself. 2.6 Common Pitfalls Trusting a data collection routine simply because records arrive consistently and on time, without ever spot-checking a sample against an independent count, allows a quiet gap between recorded figures and actual reality to persist for months or years unnoticed. Records arriving on schedule says nothing on its own about whether the figures inside them are accurate. 2.7 The Registers Had Always Looked Complete Furaha's five registers had never actually looked incomplete or suspicious on their own. The gap only became visible the moment an independent count was placed directly next to a recorded figure. 3.0 Study Session Summary and Conclusion In this study session, you learned to spot-check a data collection routine against independent reality rather than trusting it by default. Study Session 3 turns from collecting trustworthy data to writing a progress report a specific reader can actually act on.

Reflect and Grow — Self-Assessment 1. Think of a data collection routine you currently rely on. Have you ever spot-checked a sample of it against an independent count, or only trusted that it arrives on time? 2. Identify one figure in your own current reporting that has never been independently verified, and describe a simple way you could check it this month. Practical Output: Practical Output A short data quality spot-check plan for one real data collection routine, including a standardised recording tool and a schedule for independent verification. 7.0 References and Further Reading Yourkavitch, J., Prosnitz, D., & Herrera, S. (2019). Data quality assessments stimulate improvements to health management information systems: evidence from five African countries. Journal of Global Health, 9(1), 010806. Optional further reading, curriculum-team reviewed: Proverbs 11:1, on a false balance being an abomination to the Lord, while a just weight is his delight. Qur'an, Surah Ar-Rahman 55:9, on establishing weight in justice and not making the balance deficient.
Evidence to keep Keep a written note, worksheet, reflection or practical output from this study session. Your progress should show real learning before the quiz.

lessons.title: Study Session 3: Writing a Progress Report a Reader Can Act On

blocks.text: Introduction Boitumelo Mokoena, who raises two children alone while coordinating a youth skills programme in Rustenburg, produced a technically thorough thirty-page quarterly report that sat unopened in her programme director's inbox for six weeks, until a single conversation revealed the director had needed one specific figure from it and had simply given up looking. 1.0 Learning Outcomes By the end of this study session, you should be able to: Explain what research found about what actually makes an evaluation or report get used by decision makers. Distinguish a report built for general completeness from one built for a specific, intended use. Apply a method for identifying who will use a report and what decision it needs to inform, before writing it. Recognise when a technically accurate report is nonetheless failing to reach or influence its intended reader. Write a progress report section that leads with what a specific reader needs to decide or do. 2.0 Main Content 2.1 Thirty Pages, One Question, No Answer Found Boitumelo Mokoena coordinates a youth skills training programme in Rustenburg, and her quarterly reports were, by any technical measure, thorough, thirty pages covering every activity, every indicator, every site visit. When her programme director finally admitted, six weeks after one report's submission, that she had never actually found the one figure she needed from it to decide whether to renew a struggling training partner's contract, Boitumelo realised thoroughness and usefulness were not the same thing. 2.2 What Actually Makes a Report Get Used In 1997, the evaluation researcher Michael Quinn Patton set out, in Utilization-Focused Evaluation, findings from his study of federal health evaluations that traced why some evaluation reports were genuinely used by decision makers while other, equally rigorous reports were not. His conclusion, which he termed the personal factor, was that use depended far less on a report's methodological completeness than on whether specific, identified people had been engaged from the start around specific, intended decisions the findings were meant to inform. 2.3 Structuring a Report Around Its Actual Reader Naming the Specific Reader and Decision Before Writing Identifying, before drafting begins, exactly who will read a report and what specific decision or action it needs to inform, rather than writing toward a general and undefined audience, reflects the personal factor Patton's research found separated used reports from unused ones. Leading With the Answer, Not Burying It Opening a report section with the specific figure or finding a named reader actually needs, rather than requiring that reader to locate it somewhere inside a longer narrative, makes the difference between a report that gets read for its answer and one that gets abandoned before reaching it. 2.4 Key Practices Name the specific reader and the specific decision a report needs to inform before drafting it. Open each report section with the answer or figure the reader actually needs. Keep supporting detail available but secondary to the reader's specific question. Confirm directly with the intended reader, after delivery, whether the report actually answered their question. Resist adding thoroughness that no specific reader has actually asked for. 2.5 A Worked Example: Boitumelo's Reader-First Report For the following quarter, Boitumelo asked her director directly what specific decision the report needed to support, the training partner's contract renewal, and restructured the opening section around that single question, stating the partner's completion and placement rates for the quarter in the first paragraph before any narrative detail followed. Her director read the new report's opening section within minutes of receiving it and made the renewal decision the same week, a full quarter faster than the previous cycle. Boitumelo had not reduced the amount of real information behind her report. She had simply stopped assuming a thorough document and a useful one were automatically the same thing. 2.6 Common Pitfalls Writing a report toward general completeness, without first identifying a specific reader and the specific decision that reader needs to make, produces a document that is technically accurate and practically unread. A report nobody uses provides no real accountability, no matter how detailed it is. 2.7 The Report Had Never Actually Been Wrong Boitumelo's original thirty-page report had never contained inaccurate information. It had simply been organised around covering every topic completely, rather than around the one specific question a specific reader actually needed answered. 3.0 Study Session Summary and Conclusion In this study session, you learned to structure a progress report around a specific reader and the decision it needs to inform. Study Session 4 turns from writing a usable report to recognising when a programme's own indicators are quietly drifting away from its actual objective.

Reflect and Grow — Self-Assessment 1. Think of a recent report you wrote or received. Was it built around a specific reader's specific question, or around general topic completeness? 2. Identify the specific decision your next progress report needs to inform, and draft an opening section that leads directly with the answer that decision requires. Practical Output: Practical Output A restructured opening section for one real progress report, built around a named reader and the specific decision it needs to inform. 7.0 References and Further Reading Patton, M.Q. (1997). Utilization-Focused Evaluation: The New Century Text (3rd ed.). Thousand Oaks, CA: Sage Publications. Optional further reading, curriculum-team reviewed: Luke 8:16-17, on no one lighting a lamp and covering it, but setting it on a stand, since nothing hidden will fail to be made known. Qur'an, Surah Al-Alaq 96:3-5, on the Most Generous, who taught by the pen, and taught man what he did not know.
Evidence to keep Keep a written note, worksheet, reflection or practical output from this study session. Your progress should show real learning before the quiz.

quiz.q: Bolanle's antenatal visit count rose every quarter while delivery complications stayed flat. What did this reveal?
options: The programme's clinics were performing poorly overall
A rising indicator does not necessarily reflect progress on the programme's actual objective
Antenatal visits have no relationship to delivery outcomes anywhere
Bolanle had made an error in her data collection process
quiz.explain: Review Study Session 1 (Choosing Indicators That Measure What Actually Matters) before continuing.

quiz.q: According to Tulloch, Possingham and Wilson's 2011 research, what must a genuinely useful indicator be?
options: Inexpensive to collect above all else
Closely linked to the actual objective, sensitive to change, and unambiguous to interpret
Collected as frequently as possible regardless of relevance
Identical to indicators used by other programmes
quiz.explain: Review Study Session 1 (Choosing Indicators That Measure What Actually Matters) before continuing.

quiz.q: What does this session recommend checking before adopting a proposed indicator?
options: Only whether it is convenient to collect
Whether it would genuinely move if the actual objective were achieved
Whether it has ever been used by another organisation
Whether it can be collected without any staff training
quiz.explain: Review Study Session 1 (Choosing Indicators That Measure What Actually Matters) before continuing.

quiz.q: Furaha discovered two of five officers had been estimating attendance rather than counting it. What did this reveal?
options: The officers were deliberately falsifying records
A data collection routine can develop a quiet, unnoticed gap between recorded figures and reality without a check in place
Attendance registers are inherently unreliable in all settings
Agricultural extension programmes should not track attendance at all
quiz.explain: Review Study Session 2 (Building a Data Collection Routine That Can Be Trusted) before continuing.

quiz.q: According to Yourkavitch, Prosnitz and Herrera's 2019 research, what did a first formal data quality assessment reliably do?
options: Confirm that existing data collection was already fully accurate
Surface specific, previously unnoticed weaknesses and prompt concrete fixes
Have no measurable effect on subsequent data collection practices
Apply only to health programmes, not other sectors
quiz.explain: Review Study Session 2 (Building a Data Collection Routine That Can Be Trusted) before continuing.

quiz.q: What does this session recommend watching for as a simple signal of estimated rather than counted data?
options: Figures that vary widely and unpredictably
Figures that cluster suspiciously around round numbers
Figures that are submitted later than expected
Figures recorded in a different colour of ink
quiz.explain: Review Study Session 2 (Building a Data Collection Routine That Can Be Trusted) before continuing.

lessons.title: Study Session 4: Spotting Programme Drift From the Indicators Themselves

blocks.text: Introduction Mariama Sarr, who leads monitoring for a rural water and sanitation programme around Kolda, watched her main water point functionality indicator climb steadily to ninety-five percent even as community complaints about actually reaching working water grew louder each quarter, a contradiction she almost dismissed before deciding to look at what the indicator was truly counting. 1.0 Learning Outcomes By the end of this study session, you should be able to: Explain what Goodhart's Law describes about the relationship between a measure and the target it becomes. Distinguish an indicator that reflects genuine progress from one that is being optimised or gamed. Apply a method for checking whether a rising indicator reflects real progress or a narrowed definition of success. Recognise the specific signs that a programme has begun managing to a number rather than its actual objective. 2.0 Main Content 2.1 Ninety-Five Percent Functional, and Yet Mariama Sarr leads monitoring for a rural water and sanitation programme working across villages around Kolda, and her programme's headline indicator, the percentage of installed water points recorded as functional, had climbed to ninety-five percent over the past year. Over the same period, complaints logged directly from communities about actually reaching a working water point on any given day had grown steadily, a contradiction that took Mariama several weeks to take seriously rather than dismiss as noise. 2.2 When a Measure Becomes a Target In his 2018 book The Tyranny of Metrics, published by Princeton University Press, the historian Jerry Muller examined a pattern now widely known as Goodhart's Law, the principle that once a measure becomes a target that people are evaluated or rewarded against, they tend to optimise directly for the measure itself rather than the underlying goal it was meant to represent. Muller documented this pattern across sectors from healthcare to education to policing, finding that a rising metric could coexist with, and even actively conceal, a genuinely worsening underlying situation. 2.3 Checking Whether an Indicator's Rise Is Real Tracing Exactly What an Indicator Counts Tracing the precise moment and rule by which an indicator is recorded, rather than trusting the summary figure alone, often reveals that a definition has quietly narrowed or shifted in a way that inflates the number without changing the underlying reality. Pairing a Headline Indicator With a Durability Check Adding a second indicator that checks whether an improvement actually persists over time, rather than relying only on a point-in-time measure, exposes the specific kind of drift Goodhart's Law describes, where a number is optimised at the moment it is recorded without lasting change behind it. 2.4 Key Practices Trace exactly what rule and moment an indicator is actually recorded against. Pair a headline indicator with a second measure checking whether the improvement persists. Treat a contradiction between an indicator and direct community or frontline reports as information, not noise. Watch for a definition that has quietly narrowed in a way that inflates the recorded figure. 2.5 A Worked Example: Mariama's Durability Indicator Mariama discovered that field teams had begun recording a repaired water point as functional the moment repair work finished, with no follow-up check for whether it stayed working, so she added a second indicator tracking the percentage of water points still functional ninety days after any repair. The new indicator immediately told a different story: barely sixty percent of repaired points were still functional after ninety days, a figure the original headline measure had never been able to reveal because it only ever looked at the moment repairs finished. The ninety-five percent figure had never been falsified. It had simply been measuring the wrong moment in time. 2.6 Common Pitfalls Treating a rising headline indicator as sufficient evidence of genuine progress, without ever tracing exactly what moment and rule it is recorded against, allows a programme to drift from its actual objective while its own reporting continues to look reassuring. A number can be technically accurate and still conceal the problem it was meant to catch. 2.7 The Drift Had Been Inside the Definition All Along Nobody on Mariama's team had stopped caring about lasting water access. The definition behind the programme's main indicator had simply drifted toward measuring the easiest moment to record, rather than the outcome the programme genuinely existed to deliver. 3.0 Study Session Summary and Conclusion In this study session, you learned to check whether a rising indicator reflects genuine progress or a narrowed definition concealing programme drift. Study Session 5 turns from spotting drift in the indicators themselves to handling incomplete or conflicting data honestly.

Reflect and Grow — Self-Assessment 1. Think of an indicator in your own work that has been consistently rising. Have you traced exactly what moment and rule it is recorded against? 2. Identify one headline indicator you rely on, and describe a durability or follow-up check that could reveal whether its improvement genuinely persists. Practical Output: Practical Output A written trace of exactly what one real programme indicator counts, and a proposed durability or follow-up check to test whether its recorded improvement genuinely persists. 7.0 References and Further Reading Muller, J.Z. (2018). The Tyranny of Metrics. Princeton, NJ: Princeton University Press. Optional further reading, curriculum-team reviewed: Matthew 6:22-23, on the eye being the lamp of the body, and how great the darkness is if the light within is actually darkness. Qur'an, Surah Al-Kahf 18:103-104, on the greatest losers being those whose effort is lost while they think they are doing well.
Evidence to keep Keep a written note, worksheet, reflection or practical output from this study session. Your progress should show real learning before the quiz.

lessons.title: Study Session 5: Handling Incomplete or Conflicting Data Honestly

blocks.text: Introduction Abrehet Weldu, who has low vision and works through screen-reading software as a data analyst for a nutrition programme in Mekelle, received two conflicting sets of malnutrition screening figures from two field teams covering the same district for the same month, and found that the version already sitting in the draft donor report had simply used whichever number arrived first. 1.0 Learning Outcomes By the end of this study session, you should be able to: Explain what research found about the importance of transparently reporting missing or conflicting data. Apply a method for documenting a genuine data conflict rather than silently resolving it in a report. Recognise when a report is concealing genuine uncertainty behind an artificially clean number. 2.0 Main Content 2.1 Two Figures, One District, No Note of the Difference Abrehet Weldu analyses screening data for a nutrition programme covering several districts around Mekelle, working primarily through screen-reading software that reads her spreadsheets and reports aloud. Reviewing one month's draft donor report, she found the malnutrition screening rate for a single district had been reported as a single clean figure, drawn from whichever of two field teams' conflicting counts happened to have been entered into the system first, with no note anywhere that a second, different figure existed at all. 2.2 Why Missing or Conflicting Data Must Be Reported, Not Hidden In 2021, the researchers Katherine Lee and colleagues published the Treatment And Reporting of Missing data in Observational Studies framework in the Journal of Clinical Epidemiology, setting out standards for how missing or conflicting data should be handled and reported in research and monitoring findings. Their central finding was that the amount, pattern and likely cause of missing or conflicting data must be reported with enough detail for a reader to judge the reliability of the resulting figure, rather than silently resolved or smoothed away before the reader ever sees it. 2.3 Documenting a Genuine Conflict Rather Than Resolving It Silently Naming Both Figures and the Likely Reason They Differ Recording both conflicting figures explicitly, along with the most likely reason they differ, rather than quietly selecting one and presenting it as settled, gives a reader the information the Lee and colleagues framework identifies as necessary for judging the reliability of a reported result. Stating What Remains Genuinely Uncertain Stating plainly, in a report itself, what a data conflict or gap means the programme does not yet know with confidence, rather than presenting an artificially clean figure, is what separates an honest report from one that conceals real uncertainty behind apparent precision. 2.4 Key Practices Record both figures explicitly when a genuine data conflict exists, rather than silently choosing one. State the most likely reason two figures differ, where it can reasonably be determined. Name plainly, in the report itself, what remains genuinely uncertain as a result. Investigate a genuine conflict promptly rather than allowing it to sit unresolved indefinitely. 2.5 A Worked Example: Abrehet's Reconciled Note Abrehet traced the two field teams' figures back to their source and found one team had screened children up to age five while the other had used a narrower cutoff of age three, a definitional difference rather than a measurement error, and rewrote the report section to state both figures explicitly alongside a one-line explanation of the age range difference. The donor's programme officer, reading the reconciled note, immediately flagged the inconsistent age cutoffs as a training gap worth addressing across all field teams the following quarter, a fix that would never have surfaced from the original single clean figure. The conflict itself had never actually been a data error. It had been two teams honestly measuring two different things under the same label. 2.6 Common Pitfalls Resolving a genuine conflict between two data sources by silently selecting one figure for a report, without documenting that a conflict existed or why, presents false precision to a reader who has no way of knowing real uncertainty was ever there. A single tidy figure can make a genuinely uncertain result look far more settled than it actually is. 2.7 The Conflict Had Been Worth More Than Either Figure Alone Abrehet's two conflicting figures had never actually needed to be collapsed into one. The disagreement between them, once documented honestly, carried more useful information for the programme than either single number could have provided on its own. 3.0 Study Session Summary and Conclusion In this study session, you learned to document a genuine data conflict transparently rather than resolving it silently. Study Session 6 closes this course by turning to how a reporting cycle is closed honestly and carried forward into the next one.

Reflect and Grow — Self-Assessment 1. Think of a time you or your team resolved a data conflict by quietly choosing one figure. What might documenting the conflict itself have revealed? 2. Identify one figure in your own current reporting that may be concealing an unresolved conflict or gap, and draft a one-line note documenting what remains uncertain about it. Practical Output: Practical Output A short reconciled report note for one real or plausible data conflict, stating both figures, the likely reason they differ, and what remains genuinely uncertain. 7.0 References and Further Reading Lee, K.J., Tilling, K., Cornish, R.P., Little, R.J.A., Bell, M.L., Goetghebeur, E., Hogan, J.W., & Carpenter, J.R. (2021). Framework for the treatment and reporting of missing data in observational studies: the Treatment And Reporting of Missing data in Observational Studies framework. Journal of Clinical Epidemiology, 134, 79 to 88. Optional further reading, curriculum-team reviewed: Deuteronomy 19:15, on a single witness not being sufficient, and a matter being confirmed on the evidence of two or three witnesses. Qur'an, Surah Yusuf 12:26-27, on the shirt torn from the front or from the back deciding between two conflicting accounts.
Evidence to keep Keep a written note, worksheet, reflection or practical output from this study session. Your progress should show real learning before the quiz.

lessons.title: Study Session 6: Closing a Reporting Cycle and Setting Up the Next One

blocks.text: Introduction Namwene Mubanga coordinates a livelihoods programme in Kasama, and the closing report her team submitted at the end of every quarter listed exactly what had been delivered against the workplan and nothing else, with no section anywhere asking what the quarter had actually taught the team about the assumptions their own plan had been built on. 1.0 Learning Outcomes By the end of this study session, you should be able to: Explain what research found about the difference between monitoring built only for upward accountability and monitoring built for collective learning. Distinguish a closing report that only counts delivery from one that also captures what was learned. Apply a simple method for carrying a genuine lesson from one reporting cycle into the design of the next. Recognise when a reporting cycle has closed without anyone actually asking what was learned. 2.0 Main Content 2.1 Everything Delivered, Nothing Learned On Paper Namwene Mubanga coordinates a livelihoods and small enterprise support programme across several villages near Kasama, and her team's quarterly closing reports were, delivery-wise, always complete: every planned training held, every planned grant disbursed, every activity checked off against the original workplan. Not one of those reports, across two full years, had ever included a section asking what the quarter had revealed about whether the programme's own underlying assumptions still held. 2.2 Monitoring for Accountability Versus Monitoring for Learning In her 2008 doctoral thesis Seeking Surprise, completed at Wageningen University, the researcher Irene Guijt examined monitoring practice in rural resource management programmes and found that monitoring built only to satisfy upward accountability reporting, confirming that planned activities happened, systematically missed its potential as a basis for genuine collective learning. Her finding was that a reporting cycle closed well only when it deliberately asked what had actually been learned, including genuine surprises that contradicted the programme's original assumptions, not only what had been delivered on schedule. 2.3 Closing a Cycle in a Way That Feeds the Next One Asking What Genuinely Surprised the Team This Cycle Asking directly, at the close of a reporting cycle, what result or reaction genuinely surprised the team relative to what the original plan had assumed, rather than only confirming that planned activities occurred, is the exact habit Guijt's research found separated learning-oriented monitoring from accountability-only monitoring. Writing the Lesson Directly Into the Next Cycle's Plan Recording a genuine lesson from a closing cycle as a specific, named change to the following cycle's plan, rather than leaving it as an interesting observation buried in a report nobody revisits, is what actually carries learning forward rather than letting it end with the report itself. 2.4 Key Practices Ask, at the close of every cycle, what genuinely surprised the team relative to the original plan's assumptions. Include a specific learning section in a closing report, separate from the delivery checklist. Write a genuine lesson directly into the next cycle's plan as a named, specific change. Distinguish a delivery report, confirming activities happened, from a learning report, capturing what was found. 2.5 A Worked Example: Namwene's Learning Section Namwene added a short, mandatory section to her team's closing report template titled What Surprised Us This Quarter, and the first cycle it was used, a field officer noted that grant recipients who had received a short business mentoring session alongside their capital grant were repaying informal supplier debts noticeably faster than those who had received capital alone, a pattern the original workplan had never anticipated or tracked. That single observation became a specific, named change in the following quarter's plan, pairing every future capital grant with a mentoring session as standard practice rather than an occasional extra. The delivery checklist from the earlier quarters had never actually been dishonest. It had simply never asked the one question capable of turning a completed activity into an actual improvement to the programme itself. 2.6 Common Pitfalls Closing a reporting cycle with only a delivery checklist confirming that planned activities occurred, without a deliberate section asking what the team actually learned, allows a programme to repeat the same assumptions cycle after cycle even when direct evidence to revise them was sitting inside the team's own data the entire time. Confirming that activities were delivered says nothing about whether the team actually understood why they worked or did not. 2.7 The Learning Had Been There Every Quarter. Nobody Had Asked For It. Namwene's earlier closing reports had never actually lacked useful information. The information had simply never been asked for directly, sitting unrecorded in field officers' informal observations rather than in any section a report template made room for. 3.0 Study Session Summary and Conclusion In this study session, you learned to close a reporting cycle with a genuine account of what was learned, feeding directly into the next cycle's plan. This closes Course 101 and prepares you for Course 102, Data Systems and Reporting Tools for Programmes, the next course in Pathway 42.

Reflect and Grow — Self-Assessment 1. Think of a reporting cycle your own team recently closed. Did it include a genuine account of what was learned, or only a record of what was delivered? 2. Design a short learning section for your own next closing report, and identify one specific change it could feed directly into the following cycle's plan. Practical Output: Practical Output A closing report template with an added learning section, and one specific, named change carried forward into a proposed next-cycle plan. 7.0 References and Further Reading Guijt, I. (2008). Seeking Surprise: Rethinking Monitoring for Collective Learning in Rural Resource Management (doctoral thesis). Wageningen University, Wageningen, The Netherlands. Optional further reading, curriculum-team reviewed: Ecclesiastes 7:8, on the end of a matter being better than its beginning. Qur'an, Surah Ya-Sin 36:38, on the sun running its course to a determined place, set by the decree of the Exalted in Might, the Knowing.
Evidence to keep Keep a written note, worksheet, reflection or practical output from this study session. Your progress should show real learning before the quiz.

quiz.q: Mariama's functionality indicator rose to ninety-five percent while community complaints grew. What did this ultimately reveal?
options: The community complaints were unrelated to the programme
A rising headline indicator can conceal genuine programme drift when its definition has narrowed
Water point repairs had actually stopped happening entirely
Mariama's monitoring system was collecting fabricated data
quiz.explain: Review Study Session 4 (Spotting Programme Drift From the Indicators Themselves) before continuing.

quiz.q: According to Muller's account of Goodhart's Law, what tends to happen once a measure becomes a target?
options: The underlying goal automatically improves alongside the measure
People tend to optimise for the measure itself rather than the underlying goal it represents
The measure becomes permanently more accurate over time
Targets have no meaningful effect on how a measure is pursued
quiz.explain: Review Study Session 4 (Spotting Programme Drift From the Indicators Themselves) before continuing.

quiz.q: What does this session recommend pairing with a headline indicator?
options: A second indicator with no relationship to the first
A durability check confirming whether an improvement actually persists over time
A reduction in the frequency of measurement
An indicator borrowed directly from an unrelated programme
quiz.explain: Review Study Session 4 (Spotting Programme Drift From the Indicators Themselves) before continuing.

quiz.q: Abrehet found a district's screening rate had been reported as a single figure chosen from two conflicting field team counts. What did this reveal?
options: One of the two field teams had fabricated its data
A genuine data conflict was being silently resolved rather than documented for the reader
Malnutrition screening data cannot ever be reconciled across teams
The donor report should have been cancelled entirely
quiz.explain: Review Study Session 5 (Handling Incomplete or Conflicting Data Honestly) before continuing.

quiz.q: According to the Lee and colleagues 2021 framework, what must be reported about missing or conflicting data?
options: Nothing; such data should simply be excluded from reports
Its amount, pattern and likely cause, in enough detail for a reader to judge the result's reliability
Only the final resolved figure, without further explanation
Missing data should always be replaced with an estimated average
quiz.explain: Review Study Session 5 (Handling Incomplete or Conflicting Data Honestly) before continuing.

quiz.q: What does this session recommend doing when two figures genuinely conflict?
options: Selecting the higher of the two figures automatically
Recording both figures explicitly along with the most likely reason they differ
Discarding both figures and reporting no data for that period
Averaging the two figures without further comment
quiz.explain: Review Study Session 5 (Handling Incomplete or Conflicting Data Honestly) before continuing.

finalQuiz.q: Bolanle's antenatal visit count rose every quarter while delivery complications stayed flat. What did this reveal?
options: The programme's clinics were performing poorly overall
A rising indicator does not necessarily reflect progress on the programme's actual objective
Antenatal visits have no relationship to delivery outcomes anywhere
Bolanle had made an error in her data collection process
finalQuiz.explain: Review Study Session 1 (Choosing Indicators That Measure What Actually Matters) before continuing.

finalQuiz.q: According to Tulloch, Possingham and Wilson's 2011 research, what must a genuinely useful indicator be?
options: Inexpensive to collect above all else
Closely linked to the actual objective, sensitive to change, and unambiguous to interpret
Collected as frequently as possible regardless of relevance
Identical to indicators used by other programmes
finalQuiz.explain: Review Study Session 1 (Choosing Indicators That Measure What Actually Matters) before continuing.

finalQuiz.q: What does this session recommend checking before adopting a proposed indicator?
options: Only whether it is convenient to collect
Whether it would genuinely move if the actual objective were achieved
Whether it has ever been used by another organisation
Whether it can be collected without any staff training
finalQuiz.explain: Review Study Session 1 (Choosing Indicators That Measure What Actually Matters) before continuing.

finalQuiz.q: Furaha discovered two of five officers had been estimating attendance rather than counting it. What did this reveal?
options: The officers were deliberately falsifying records
A data collection routine can develop a quiet, unnoticed gap between recorded figures and reality without a check in place
Attendance registers are inherently unreliable in all settings
Agricultural extension programmes should not track attendance at all
finalQuiz.explain: Review Study Session 2 (Building a Data Collection Routine That Can Be Trusted) before continuing.

finalQuiz.q: According to Yourkavitch, Prosnitz and Herrera's 2019 research, what did a first formal data quality assessment reliably do?
options: Confirm that existing data collection was already fully accurate
Surface specific, previously unnoticed weaknesses and prompt concrete fixes
Have no measurable effect on subsequent data collection practices
Apply only to health programmes, not other sectors
finalQuiz.explain: Review Study Session 2 (Building a Data Collection Routine That Can Be Trusted) before continuing.

finalQuiz.q: What does this session recommend watching for as a simple signal of estimated rather than counted data?
options: Figures that vary widely and unpredictably
Figures that cluster suspiciously around round numbers
Figures that are submitted later than expected
Figures recorded in a different colour of ink
finalQuiz.explain: Review Study Session 2 (Building a Data Collection Routine That Can Be Trusted) before continuing.

finalQuiz.q: Boitumelo's thorough thirty-page report sat unread for six weeks. What did this reveal?
options: The report contained inaccurate information
A technically thorough report is not automatically a used one if it is not built around a specific reader's need
Youth skills programmes should not produce written reports
The programme director was not interested in the programme's progress
finalQuiz.explain: Review Study Session 3 (Writing a Progress Report a Reader Can Act On) before continuing.

finalQuiz.q: According to Patton's research described in this session, what did he term the factor separating used evaluation reports from unused ones?
options: The methodology factor
The personal factor
The length factor
The funding factor
finalQuiz.explain: Review Study Session 3 (Writing a Progress Report a Reader Can Act On) before continuing.

finalQuiz.q: What does the personal factor concept emphasise?
options: Methodological rigour above all other considerations
Specific, identified people engaged from the start around specific, intended uses
Reports should always be as long and detailed as possible
Evaluation findings should never be shared with decision makers directly
finalQuiz.explain: Review Study Session 3 (Writing a Progress Report a Reader Can Act On) before continuing.

options: The community complaints were unrelated to the programme
A rising headline indicator can conceal genuine programme drift when its definition has narrowed
Water point repairs had actually stopped happening entirely
Mariama's monitoring system was collecting fabricated data
finalQuiz.explain: Review Study Session 4 (Spotting Programme Drift From the Indicators Themselves) before continuing.
